title: Royal Street Rattler
subtitle: a Dixieland strut for six players
concept: the rattle of a 1924 New Orleans streetcar, taught to strut by the band on the corner.
about: Royal Street, late afternoon, 1924. A streetcar rattles toward the river, iron wheels clicking over the rail joints in a syncopation that never lands where you expect. On the corner, a six-piece band catches the rhythm out of the air — and by the second chorus every pedestrian on the block has stopped walking and started strutting.

The whole piece grows from that one cell: three repeated notes and a leap onto the offbeat, stated by woodblock before a single horn plays. It becomes the F-major Strut, turns minor under the balconies where the trombone growls, and rides out to the river in B♭, where the passengers tell their stories — a kid weaving through the crowd (clarinet), a riverboat man leaning on a post (tenor sax), the bandleader showing off in stop-time (trumpet).

I composed every melody, solo, and break note-by-note in Python, and let small constrained generators do what real bands do by formula: banjo four-to-the-bar, two-beat sousaphone with walkups, clarinet obbligato that fills the lead's holes, tailgate trombone with real pitch-bend smears. Swing is a timeline warp — offbeat eighths at 57.5% of the beat, the light fast swing of a street band, not a metronome's triplets.

Dixieland is conversation music: three melodic voices improvising at once without stepping on each other, over a rhythm section that never stops grinning. This is a transcription of one such conversation, on one good corner, at sundown.

movements.title: Royal Street Rattler
movements.note: one continuous strut: three strains, three solos, a drum break, and the classic three-break tag.
sections: the kid in the crowd — clarinet

moments.text: the hook arrives as pure percussion — three clicks and a leap, a wheel crossing a rail joint.
stop-time: the band drops to single hits and the leader talks in the gaps.
the sousaphone breaks into a four-beat walk — the floor starts moving.
trombone, clarinet, trumpet — two beats of fame each. then two hits, one chord, and the streetcar plops off around the corner.
